comment.narrative: 3 reports produced. Desk research preceded the baseline study, and was focused on analysing secondary data. The objective of the desk research was to analyse existing country-level, context-specific data on the sexual and gender-based violence and political participation of two key constituencies to WGG: young women and girls and women with disabilities in five countries: Bangladesh, India, Kenya, Rwanda and Uganda. Desk research was designed to guide the baseline study especially by informing methodologies, its scope and focus. It was essential to understand young women and girls and women with disabilities are not homogenous categories. The research addressed data disaggregated to the extent possible by e.g. different disabilities, age, living in rural/urban areas, women living in institutions etc. Key resources included in analysis were governmental data, national statistical organisation data, census data, academic papers, autonomous research bodies research, national and international non-governmental organisations reports (including development sector reports) and media resources. Both qualitative and quantitative data were reported. The desk research resulted in three separate reports focused on East Africa (Rwanda, Kenya, Uganda), Bangladesh and India, summarising data as well as identifying gaps in existing data on GBV and political participation and the two constituencies WGG works with.

IWRAW AP work on "Anti-Carceral Approaches to SGBV and the Political Participation of Young Women and Women with Disabilities" was delivered only in 2023. It is a final research report prepared by Kemban Kolektif.

In 2024, the WGG Consortium organised nine learning sessions to strengthen the capacity of all partner organisations. Five learning docs were produced from these learning sessions. 1) history of feminist movements in Bangladesh, Kenya, Rwanda, and Uganda, 2) Decolonization and GBV with a focus on EA , 3) Gender Transformative Approaches and how they can centre structurally excluded groups, 4) understanding feminist MEL 5) Gender equality and macroeconomics (GEM).

Learning Paper- With five feminist, disability justice activists, the WGG CREA team co-authored a learning paper titled ‘Invisibilised Gender-Based Violence Against Diverse Women, Girls, and Gender-Diverse Persons with Disabilities in the Global South’ in 2025. The paper highlights how specific and often invisibilised forms of gender-based violence disproportionately impact diverse women, girls, and gender-diverse persons with disabilities (DW&GWD). It deploys the participatory methodology of storytelling and reflective circles to centre experiences of the denial of legal capacity, manifestations of GBV in political participation, culture and religious norms as drivers of GBV, violence in sexual and reproductive health and rights and medical spaces, and caregiver and Intimate Partner Violence. The research for the paper involved over 50 activists and disability justice professionals across 13 countries in South and Southeast Asia, and East and Southern Africa. These also served as much-needed spaces for healing, solidarity, and connection. The paper calls for the meaningful integration of the needs and rights of DW&GWD into the GBV prevention and response work. The paper is due for publication in March 2026.Stories of Change- This participatory monitoring and evaluation approach adopted by the Consortium has helped archive the Most Significant Changes in the lives of individuals, in policies, practices, and organisational structures. The stories were collected through interviews, photography, focus group discussions, and observation, with careful attention to ethical considerations around consent, safety, and appropriate representation of marginalised voices. The stories document eight critical transformation patterns that emerged in WGG's work: (1) the evolution from isolated organisations to cross-movement solidarity; (2) the transformation of program participants into independent feminist movement leaders who formed youth-led collectives with their own funding and agendas; (3) shift from service delivery to policy influence and systems change, with Strategic Partners launching campaigns, improving policies, and engaging directly with government officials; (4) paradigm shift from charity-based to rights-based disability advocacy through the DSROI; (5) evolution from silo-ed organisational work to collective feminist political vision, marked by critical discussions and sophisticated approaches to GBV; (6) from individual suffering to collective action in SGBV response; (7) from exclusion to creation of feminist initiatives; and (8) from personal struggle to disability rights expertise and systemic change advocacy.Lasting outcomes include the formation of cross-movement partnerships, feminist spaces and initiatives, enhanced organisational practices and intersectional approaches, and improved cross-movement dialogue and understanding. Skills developed through these programs—partnership brokering, empathetic engagement, intersectional analysis, and cross-movement solidarity building—continue to strengthen feminist movements across East Africa and South Asia.
